loan-payoff-calculator.formula:
Monthly rate r = APR / 12 / 100
Each month: interest = balance x r; principal paid = payment - interest; new balance = balance - principal paid.
Months to payoff is about -ln(1 - balance x r / payment) / ln(1 + r). Simulated month-by-month here.
howTo: Enter your current loan balance and APR.
Enter any extra amount you can pay each month (0 is fine).
Compare: months to payoff, total interest, and what the extra payment saves you.
Adjust the extra payment to find a payoff date that fits your goals.
keyFacts: Every payment splits into interest (on the remaining balance) and principal (which shrinks the balance).
Extra payments go 100% to principal, so each one also wipes out all the future interest that principal would have earned.
Paying $100 extra monthly often beats a yearly lump sum - the money starts working sooner.
Check for prepayment penalties before accelerating; most personal loans and US mortgages have none.
Attack the highest-rate debt first - a dollar of extra payment saves the most interest there.
Even rounding your payment up ($293 to $300) compounds into real savings over years.

loan-payoff-calculator.quickAnswer: Extra payments attack principal directly, shrinking both the payoff time and total interest. For example, on a $10,000 loan at 12% APR paying $200 a month, adding $100 extra cuts payoff from about 70 months to 41 - saving roughly 29 months and $1,706 in interest. Try your own numbers below.

loan-payoff-calculator.workedExample:
$10,000 balance, 12% APR, $200/month, +$100 extra:
1. Monthly rate = 1%. Base payment $200, accelerated $300.
2. Without extra: about 70 months, about $3,931 total interest.
3. With $100 extra: about 41 months, about $2,225 total interest.
4. You save about 29 months and about $1,706 in interest.
